figures.caption: Figure 1: End-to-end neuromorphic decoding of dynamic vision from retinal ganglion cell populations. (a) Visual stimuli, flashed natural or synthetic images (400 ms) or moving targets (2-s clips of randomly moving digits, bars and gratings), are projected onto (b) an ex vivo mouse retina on a CMOS high-density microelectrode array, yielding spike-sorted RGC units. (c) Population spikes (raster of one held-out clip; colors mark ON, OFF and ON–OFF cells) are placed at each cell’s receptive-field center with a Gaussian kernel, giving a [T ×3×32×32] input tensor with one channel per polarity. (d) A single spike-native decoder, a shared spiking encoder with a reconstruction readout and a tracking readout, built from leaky or non-leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF/IF) neurons and trained with surrogate gradients; its sparse, event-driven computation uses a small fraction of the compute energy of the equivalent ANN decoder (Sec. 4.6) and can map onto neuromorphic hardware. (e) Its outputs: the reconstructed stimulus (a flashed synthetic pattern and a moving digit; masked-SSIM 0.81 natural and 0.88 synthetic, SSIM 0.80 for moving digits) and the target position at every time step (decoded, teal; true path, dashed; 1.33 px mean error over 300 held-out clips). The moving-digit example is the same held-out clip as in Figs. 3 and 7.

Figure 2: Ex vivo retina MEA recording and data preparation. (a) Schematic of ex vivo retina MEA recording testbed. Up to 1836 cells were recorded from a piece of retina (2 mm × 2 mm) by the array, with visual stimuli delivered by a Digital Light Processor (DLP) at a wavelength of 405 nm. (b) After spike sorting, the mean pairwise correlation coefficient across trials was calculated for each unit, and units with a mean correlation coefficient greater than 0.2 (dashed line) were retained as high-quality units; one curve per recording batch, units ranked by correlation. (c) Receptive fields (RF) of three representative cells of different types: responses over the 20× 20 mapping grid in the ON and OFF windows. (d) Receptive-field centers of the 1206 cells of the moving-digit recording on the 32× 32 input grid, colored by response polarity (ON, OFF, ON–OFF; the color key of (c) and Figs. 1c and 7a). Left: the continuous (sub-pixel) centers, at which each cell’s firing rate is rendered with a unit-mass Gaussian kernel (Gaussian splatting; Methods) to form the decoder input. Right: the same centers snapped to the nearest grid pixel (hard snap), shown for comparison; cells that share a pixel are merged.

Figure 3: Shared-encoder dual-head spiking network architecture. (a) Input spike maps (1206 RGCs, ON/OFF/ON–OFF channels, T = 200 bins) pass through an optional MA-SNN attention front-end [33] (purple; moving-digit models only) into a shared SEW-ResNet [34] spiking U-Net encoder (teal; DS, 2× 2 max-pool). Its multiscale features feed (i) the reconstruction submodule (orange; US, nearest-neighbor ×2 with concatenated skips), whose output neuron never fires and whose membrane V [t] is fused over time and passed through a sigmoid, and (ii) the tracking submodule (blue), which adds a full-resolution regression offset to a spike-count centroid. Apart from the input stage (the optional attention module and the first convolution, which read the RF-mapped input), every stage is spiking (LIF/IF neurons; red symbols mark spike tensors); gray blocks are analog readout operations and the dotted line marks the spiking/analog boundary. The same weights are applied at every time step (nested frames). Parameter counts are printed per block: 5.9 M for the moving-digit model and 5.4 M for the flashed-image model (1836 cells, T = 80, no attention, 512-pixel output). Thumbnails: running readout σ(V [t]) at t = 50, 100 and 199, and the fused reconstruction of one held-out clip (digit 3). (b) Block definitions and legend.

Figure 4: Image reconstruction of flashed stimuli decoded from 1836 RGCs by the end-to-end spiking U-Net. Ground truth (left) versus spike-native reconstruction (right), 7× 8 held-out examples per panel, for (a) synthetic patterns (masked-SSIM 0.88) and (b) natural images (masked-SSIM 0.81). Similarity index is quoted over all 200 held-out images.

Table 1: Reconstruction fidelity versus model size on flashed natural-image decoding from 1836 RGC spiking neurons. All models decode the same held-out receptive-field-mapped input. Parameters are measured by torchinfo for the spiking decoders; † denotes published architecture size for the artificial-network refiners. Masked-SSIM values are given on the shared held-out test set.

Figure 5: Reconstruction fidelity versus model size, and compute energy. (a) Reconstruction fidelity (masked-SSIM, window 11, 512 px, n = 200 held-out images, identical protocol for every point) versus model size for 18 decoders on the same 1836-RGC flashed natural-image task: our spiking U-Net (teal star), other spiking models (light teal) and artificial networks (gray); circles decode the RGC input directly, squares refine the Meta-SpikeFormer decode, diamonds are generative models. Fidelity saturates in a narrow band (shaded, interquartile range of the 18 models) across more than two orders of magnitude in parameter count, suggesting a neural-data-limited rather than capacity-limited regime; the spiking U-Net of this paper (star, ∼5.4M parameters) reaches this band with 5.5–11× fewer parameters than the spiking-transformer decoders. Models 1–5 lie within 0.003 SSIM of each other and are numbered (markers 2 and 3, both 17M, are offset horizontally for visibility); † published architecture size; spiking-model parameters measured by torchinfo. (b) Compute energy per sample under a 45 nm convention (multiply–accumulate 4.6 pJ, accumulate 0.9 pJ): the ANN-equivalent (dense multiply–accumulates), the same spike-driven operation count at multiply–accumulate cost, and the spike-native network (synaptic operations at accumulate cost); the ∼70× reduction factorizes into ∼13.6× fewer operations (spike sparsity at 14.2% mean firing) and ∼5.1× cheaper operations. (c) Spike-driven energy by module for the reported model (λ = 0) and a model trained with a firing-rate penalty (λ = 0.1): the penalty removes 21% of the synaptic operations (∼70× → ∼88×) at a reconstruction cost (validation SSIM 0.80 → 0.73; separate training runs). (d) Firing rate of every spiking layer for the two models: the penalty lowers firing in the decoder, where fan-out is largest, and raises it in the tracking head, so the mean rate is unchanged while synaptic operations fall. The output-head neuron never fires and is not shown. Energy estimates are compute-only (memory movement excluded).

Figure 6: Reconstruction of moving bars and drifting gratings recorded and decoded from spiking RGC populations. (a) Moving bar, 45◦ (diagonal) direction, one held-out trial: ground truth (top) and spike-native reconstruction (bottom) at eight times while the bar crosses the recorded patch. (b) SSIM (window 3) versus time within a sweep (bars, top) or condition (gratings, bottom), mean ± s.d. over directions or conditions and trials; shading marks the bar inside the patch and the 2 s drift (light blue) and the blank after the drift (gray). (c) Bars: SSIM per motion direction over windows with the bar inside the patch (mean ± s.d., four held-out trials). (d) Gratings: SSIM during the drift (teal) and reconstruction-to-stimulus contrast ratio (open squares) for all 40 conditions (8 directions × 5 temporal frequencies at a spatial frequency of 0.4 cycles per degree); lines join means over directions. Reconstruction is faithful up to 4 Hz, degrades at 8 Hz and fails at 15 Hz. (e) Ground truth (top) and reconstruction (bottom) mid-drift for one direction at 1, 4, 8 and 15 Hz, with the SSIM of each condition. The reconstructions are the model output at the end of each causal sliding window (10 bins, 100 ms, for the bars; 3 bins, 30 ms, for the gratings; Methods).

Figure 7: (Continued.) (a) RGC population spike maps over time (ON, OFF and ON–OFF cells in terracotta, blue and green, the color key of Figs. 1c and 2; spikes accumulated over 50 ms windows). (b) The running reconstruction refines over time: the image is diffuse and of low contrast early into the video clip; the moving digit emerges as the spiking membranes accumulate evidence during motion (SSIM against the ground-truth digit under each frame). (c) The final reconstruction closely matches the ground-truth digit. (d) Reconstruction sharpens systematically as spiking evidence accumulates: mean ± s.d. reconstruction SSIM (window-3, versus the ground-truth digit) of the running membrane readout σ(mem[t]) at each timestep, averaged over all 300 held-out clips (teal), together with the curve of the clip shown in (a)–(c) (dashed). The estimate is diffuse early in the clip (SSIM near zero at 100 ms), rises through the 1.6 s motion phase as the spiking membranes integrate evidence, and plateaus at ∼0.80 by the end of motion, holding through the 0.4 s blank (shaded). The plateau matches the reported single-forward-pass reconstruction quality, consistent with the sharpening reflecting temporal evidence accumulation rather than a single informative frame. (e) Final SSIM of every held-out clip by digit class (dots), the median per class (black) and the overall mean (dashed; n = 300). (f) Cumulative reconstruction ablation (Table 2; separate training runs): spiking centroid baseline, adding the attention front-end, adding the temporal-fusion readout. Position tracking from the same encoder is quantified and assessed separately in Fig. 9.
Table 2: Component ablation on dynamic-MNIST decoding. Rows are separate training runs.

Figure 9: The SNN outperforms a calibrated center-of-mass readout in tracking a randomly moving object. (a) Mean ± s.d. position error (32-grid px) over the 300 held-out clips for each readout: chance (predict-center, 9.10 px), the calibrated center-of-mass (COM) baseline (2.91 px), the spikecount centroid readout (2.14 px) and the full-resolution spiking regression readout (1.33 px), which beats the calibrated COM baseline roughly two-fold. (b) True trajectory (dashed black; circle, start; square, end) overlaid with the decoded trajectory of the spiking regression readout (teal) and of the calibrated COM (dotted gray) for three held-out clips; the error of the spiking readout is printed above each. (c) Per-clip error versus the digit’s pixel content (ink pixels) for the calibrated COM (gray) and the spiking regression readout (teal); lines join the quintile means. Error falls as pixel content grows for both readouts, and the spiking readout stays below the COM baseline at every size. (d) Position error versus time within the clip, mean ± s.d. over clips, for the spiking regression readout and the calibrated COM; the shaded window is the target’s motion shifted by the 250 ms response latency, and curves are shown where a target position is defined. (e) Cumulative component ablation of the tracking readout (Table 2; separate training runs).
